summary: On 25 November 2020 a small capacity addition to Kinesis's front-end fleet pushed every server over an operating system thread limit. Kinesis failed for hours and took Cognito, CloudWatch, Lambda and others with it.

overview.background: Kinesis Data Streams front-end servers each keep a shard-map cache built by talking to every other front-end server. Many AWS services use Kinesis for streaming data, and CloudWatch and Cognito depend on it.
systems: Kinesis front-end fleet and its shard-map cache
AWS Lambda, Auto Scaling, ECS and EKS
overview.impact: Errors on Kinesis put and get calls from 5:15 AM PST. Cognito, CloudWatch metrics and logs, Lambda, container provisioning and Auto Scaling were all degraded, and Kinesis was fully normal at 10:23 PM PST.
overview.severity: A multi-service, region-wide event in US-EAST-1. AWS does not publish a numeric severity.
overview.gaps: The post gives no raw logs and no customer counts.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: Thread limit on every front-end server
diagrams.caption: Each front-end server builds its shard map by contacting its peers, so a bigger fleet meant more threads per server. All servers crossed the limit together.

nodes.label: Capacity added to the front-end fleet
Front-end fleet: threads over the OS limit

diagrams.title: Smaller blast radius for the front end (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: AWS said it would move to larger servers, dedicate a fleet to the shard-map cache, partition large callers and speed up cellularization. This picture shows the idea.

afterChanges: A capacity change affects one cell, not all of Kinesis.
Fewer, larger servers need fewer threads each.
A thread alarm fires long before the limit.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: A small amount of capacity is added to the front-end fleet. AWS calls this the trigger, not the root cause.
Errors appear on putting and getting Kinesis records and alarms fire.
Teams review logs and start removing the new capacity as a precaution.
The root cause is narrowed to a few candidates. Each fix needs a full front-end restart.
The cause is confirmed and recovery starts after the added capacity is removed.
The first restarted front-end servers take traffic. Traffic is added slowly.
Kinesis is fully back to normal.

rootCause.trigger: Adding servers made every existing server open more threads to talk to its peers.
rootCause.underlying: The fleet exceeded the maximum number of operating system threads, so cache construction failed and servers had unusable shard maps.
contributing: The thread limit was not alarmed
A full-fleet restart was needed, and restarts must be paced because servers rebuild caches
Cognito depended on Kinesis and could exhaust buffers
The status posting tool depended on Cognito
propagation: Every server exceeds its thread limit.
Kinesis requests fail and dependent services degrade.

evidence.label: The cause in AWS's words
evidence.body: the new capacity had caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads

evidence.label: The planned alarm
evidence.body: We are adding fine-grained alarming for thread consumption in the service.

evidence.label: A simulated thread check
evidence.note: Shows how to read thread use against the system limit. Numbers are invented.

diagnose.step: Count threads per process and compare with limits.
diagnose.why: A fleet-wide limit shows up as many hosts near the same number.

diagnose.step: Correlate the first errors with recent change events.
diagnose.why: AWS saw the capacity change first.

diagnose.step: Check whether failures are in the service or in the cache bootstrap.
diagnose.why: Servers were running but could not route.

correct.why: Each restarted server rebuilds its cache, so a mass restart can stall. AWS added traffic slowly.

correct.step: Point bootstrap at the authoritative metadata store.

verify.step: Watch the error rate fall as each group joins.
verify.why: Confirm the pool is healthy, not just running.
They recovered on their own timelines.

prevent.step: Alarm on thread count against the limit.

prevent.why: AWS said this reduces threads per server.

prevent.step: Separate big callers into partitions and cells.

prevent.why: AWS's posting tool depended on Cognito.

fix.safety: Restarting a whole fleet at once can make an outage longer. Change one group at a time and keep removing capacity as the first step.

troubleshoot.scenario: Error rates for a streaming service jump after you add servers. Servers are up but cannot route requests.
clues: All servers show the same thread count
troubleshoot.question: What do you check and in what order?
hints: What grows when the fleet grows?
Is it a bug or a limit?
troubleshoot.answer: Look at the recent change, check thread and file limits per host, roll back the change, restart in small groups while watching caches, and then verify dependents.

options: Every front-end server exceeded a thread limit after capacity was added
rootcause.why: AWS says the new capacity caused all servers to exceed the maximum number of threads.

remediation.answer: Alarm when threads in use exceed about 70 percent of the limit on any host, and page above 85 percent.
Restart a few servers, wait for caches to build, check error rate, then continue in growing steps.
Host it on infrastructure that does not use the services it reports on.

design.prompt: Design a front end that scales without every node talking to every node.
design.answer: Use cells, a dedicated cache tier, partitioned fleets for the largest callers, and limits that are alarmed.

checks.q: What did AWS call the small capacity addition?
checks.why: AWS says it was the trigger, not the root cause.

checks.q: Why was the status page delayed?
options: Its posting tool depended on Cognito, which depended on Kinesis
checks.why: AWS notes early updates were delayed for this reason.

checks.q: Why was a full restart slow?
options: Servers rebuild caches and must be added slowly
checks.why: AWS added traffic slowly as servers rebuilt.

checks.q: Which action reduces threads per server?
options: Using larger servers and fewer of them
checks.why: That is one of AWS's corrective actions.
